  "text": "After the library closed, Ruth still found borrowing slips in her coat pockets. She used them for shopping lists, writing butter beneath the names of books nobody had returned.

Her son suggested she join something.

“I belonged to the library.”

“That was a job.”

“It had chairs.”

In April, the laundrette put a bookcase beside its change machine. Ruth noticed it while washing the winter blankets. Someone had shelved a gardening manual between two crime novels, spine inward.

She corrected this.

The owner, a young man called Dev, watched from behind the counter.

“Help yourself,” he said.

“I’m not taking anything.”

“Neither is anyone else.”

The next Tuesday she brought eleven paperbacks in a shopping trolley. She arranged them while her sheets revolved behind her.

Dev offered her tea in a mug advertising brake pads.

Soon people began leaving books. Most were readable. Some had survived conditions Ruth preferred not to imagine.

She made a small sign: TAKE ONE. BRING ONE IF YOU LIKE.

“Should we keep records?” Dev asked.

“No,” she said, surprising herself.

A taxi driver asked for something short. A woman with three children wanted a book in which nobody needed looking after. Ruth considered each request carefully.

By September, she was visiting on Fridays too, without washing.

One afternoon Dev found her repairing a torn cover with tape.

“You know you don’t work here?”

“Yes.”

He put her tea on the folding table.

She pressed the tape flat with her thumbnail. Beside her, a dryer stopped, and a man looked up from his book, then lowered his eyes to finish the page."
